newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Poor returns bring Texaco, Shell together.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Poor returns bring Texaco, Shell together.

text.p: Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co, who confirmed Monday they are discussing what could be the largest downstream oil merger in United States' history, have good reason to be talking to each other after years of failed efforts to improve returns, analysts said.
"Both of these companies had only a five pct return on U.S. refining interests in the last couple of years," said Adam Sieminski, an industry analyst at NatWest Securities in Baltimore.

The two oil giants said they are discussing some combination of their U.S. downstream assets, as well as those of Star Enterprise, Texaco's joint venture with state-owned Saudi Aramco. They said they expect the talks to go on for months.

"A merger would be positive in two ways," said Steve Pfeiffer, an analyst at Paine Webber. "It would result in a cost saving of $1 billion-plus. And they would reap the benefits of having the largest market presence in the country."

A three-way combination could involve assets of approximately $17 billion. It could bring together Shell's more than 8,700 branded retail outlets with Texaco/Star's 14,000 for a 15 pct share of the national market.

Shell runs five refineries as well as a joint venture with Mexico's state oil company Petroleos Mexicanos (PEMEX) with a total refining capacity of 790,000 barrels per day, while Star and Texaco operate seven plants with total capacity of 986,000 bpd. The combined national share of refining would be 12 pct.

The fundamental reason for both companies' poor dowsntream returns -- tough competition in a refining industry with too much capacity -- shows little sign of improving. Indeed, upcoming third quarter results and refining margins so far in the fourth quarter are likely to show that it is getting worse.

"In the U.S., refining margins have been absolutely miserable in the last couple of months," said Paul Ting, oil industry analyst at Salomon Brothers. "One cannot escape the conclusion that...if there is going to be any surprise in the third quarter it is going to be weakness," Ting adds.

Big integrated oil companies' shares have been doing well in the third quarter on a soaring oil price. But gasoline prices have failed to keep pace, which has meant that overall refining margins have sunk into loss-making territory.

Salomon Brothers expects integrated oil companies to show earnings running about 10 pct lower in the third quarter compared with a good second quarter. But the quarter-on-quarter decline in the downstream end "is so outlandish -- several hundred pct -- that I haven't bothered to put a figure on it," Ting said.
"If oil prices continue to move higher it is going to maintain the pressure...and refiners are going to be the ones biggest hit," said Pfeiffer.
"This quarter underscores how really bad things are in U.S. (refining and marketing)," said Holly Gustafson, an industry analyst at NatWest Securities in Baltimore.
"The first thing (a potential merger) does is allow them to get the benefit from synergies," she said. "You'll probably see some rationalisation on the retail side."

If a merger of this size were agreed, either the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) or the Justice Department would almost certainly review it for any anti-trust implications, an FTC spokesman said on Monday.
"The FTC reaction will have very interesting implications," said Ting. "With a minimum amount of objection it would encourage other players to do the same."

Though there are very high exit costs associated with closing refining plants because of environmental regulations, proposed downstream mergers this year, including British Petroleum Co and Mobil Corp in Europe and Ultramar and Diamond Shamrock, are breaking the logjam.
Talks between Phillips Petroleum and DuPont Co unit Conoco stalled earlier this year. But Atlantic Richfield and Unocal have said they want to break out of their west coast base.

"In the last three or four years there has been only about 600,000 barrels a day of capacity taken out (of the U.S. industry)," said Ting. "This could be a very interesting litmus test of what the industry is going to do."
